commentary.seminaVerbi:
Jeroboam is the anxious improvisor who thinks control is salvation. He can’t tolerate the risk of longing, pilgrimage, distance, an authority not of his making, so he manufactures a nearer god and a nearer calendar. The calves aren’t mere bad theology; they’re a stress response. He turns dread into infrastructure. The psyche loves this move: if the heart might change, change the heart’s environment, shorten the leash, rename the substitute “deliverance.”

The man of God is the opposite failure: purity without permeability. He can refuse a king’s gift yet cannot metabolize a fellow religious voice that flatters his self-image. The old prophet is institutional ambiguity in human form, the compromised insider who knows the local game and still speaks in God-talk. The death is the story’s brutal insight: charisma doesn’t equal discernment; sincerity doesn’t protect you from suggestion. The lion that will not eat is judgment with a strange restraint, violence that feels like an enacted sentence rather than appetite.

Mark’s wilderness meal is the counter-architecture. No manufactured shrine, no coerced festival, no propaganda about who “brought you out.” Just compassion that feeds without capturing, abundance that doesn’t need a rival capital. It’s an anti-Jeroboam sign: the center holds without needing to be staged, and the people can be satisfied without being managed.

Semina Verbi, speculative: Jeroboam’s calves resemble the Hindu warning about murti becoming political instrument rather than window, when image is used to domesticate the divine for power. The old prophet’s “an angel told me” echoes Buddhist and Daoist cautions about false teachers and seductive siddhis, where spiritual language becomes a tool of control. The wilderness feeding parallels the Sikh langar’s noncoercive bread and the bodhisattva ideal of compassion that meets bodies first, as well as Sufi baraka stories where blessing multiplies food without turning the crowd into a faction.
commentary.excursus:
Jeroboam isn’t inventing new gods; he’s inventing a geography that will keep him alive. He knows desire moves on roads. Jerusalem is a magnetic center, and if bodies keep traveling there his own body ends. So he builds substitutes close enough to satisfy, loud enough to distract, and official enough to make betrayal feel like loyalty. The calves are not theology; they’re crowd-control made visible.

The “man of God” is the pure instrument, and that purity is brittle. He can face a king and split an altar, but he can’t face the softer temptation: food, shade, hospitality, the intimacy of being understood by an older colleague. The old prophet lies the way institutions lie: with credentials, with insider language, with a counterfeit “angel” that sounds like permission. The lion is not random punishment; it’s the story admitting what the prophet wouldn’t: the wilderness eats the righteous when they try to make a home inside the enemy’s house.

Mark’s wilderness is the same landscape with a different master. The disciples ask the political question—where can anyone get enough out here?—because they assume scarcity is the law. Jesus doesn’t replace Jerusalem with a calf; he refuses the whole economy of fear. He feeds them without binding them, then sends them away without taking a hostage. Jeroboam offers bread as a leash; Jesus gives bread that makes leaving possible.
commentary.synthesis: God opposes fabricated worship and the fear-politics that sustains it, judging both altar and agent. In Christ, provision flows from divine compassion rather than institutional manipulation, and abundance is ordered toward communion, not control.

gospel.text: The scene is organized around logistics that become revelation: distance (“afar off”), number (“seven”), and dismissal (“sent them away”). Jesus’ action makes provision without founding a rival shrine; he feeds, disperses, and departs—miracle without regime, abundance without cultic capture.

reading.text: The schism is stabilized by replicated forms: feast, altar, incense—continuity theater that severs the center. Into that staged continuity enters a word “by the Lord,” not as debate but as interruption, forcing the political cult to meet a transcendent audit.

Jeroboam can request prayer for his arm yet not for his throne; he seeks symptom relief, not conversion. The old prophet becomes an instrument of judgment against his own deceit, showing that divine speech can pass through compromised mouths without vindicating them; authority is not sanctity.

Bones beside bones: even the deceiver confesses the durability of the threatened word. The narrative closes with institutional inertia—sin as a house-tradition—ending not in reform but excision: dynastic policy becomes dynastic ruin.

marginalia.text: Revolt begins as interior monologue: policy incubated in fear.
“Behold thy gods”: plural cover for a single anxiety; Exodus language weaponized.
Cult is staffed downward: convenience replaces lineage; office becomes a lever.
A calendar invented “of his own heart”: counterfeit liturgy as statecraft.
Prophecy addresses the altar, not the king: judgment falls first on the machine.
The grasping hand withers mid-command: coercion collapses into impotence.
Refusal of gifts: the messenger must not be bought, even by half a house.
“An angel spoke to me”: counterfeit revelation; piety used as a forgery stamp.
Lion kills but does not consume: execution without appetite; a sign, not a meal.
Compassion stated as premise, not reaction: need is read before it speaks.
Bread-question in a wilderness: disciples trapped in scarcity logic beside abundance.
Thanks precedes fullness: Eucharistic order—gratitude before surplus.
Fragments gathered after satiety: excess is counted, not squandered.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer: O God, who enlightened the Slavic peoples through the apostolic labors of the holy brothers Cyril and Methodius, grant us the grace to accept your word and to become a people united in the confession and defense of the true faith. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God for ever and ever.

hoursOfPrayer.prayer:
Let us pray:

After First Vespers of Sunday or of solemnities that fall on Sunday:

Keep us, Lord, through this night, and grant that tomorrow, as the new day dawns, the celebration of Sunday may fill us with the joy of the resurrection of your Son. Who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

After Vespers of solemnities that do not fall on Sunday:

Visit, Lord, this room: drive far from it the snares of the enemy; let your holy angels dwell in it and keep us in peace, and may your blessing remain always with us. Through Jesus Christ our Lord.

lines: And Jeroboam said in his heart: Now shall the kingdom return to the house of David,

If this people go up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord at Jerusalem: and the heart of this people will turn to their lord Roboam, the king of Juda, and they will kill me, and return to him.

And finding out a device, he made two golden calves, and said to them: Go ye up no more to Jerusalem: Behold thy gods, O Israel, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt. Golden calves... It is likely, by making his gods in this form, he mimicked the Egyptians, among whom he had sojourned, who worshipped their Apis and their Osiris under the form of a bullock.

And he set the one in Bethel, and the other in Dan: Bethel and Dan... Bethel was a city of the tribe of Ephraim in the southern part of the dominions of Jeroboam, about six leagues from Jerusalem; Dan was in the extremity of his dominions to the north in the confines of Syria.
And this thing became an occasion of sin: for the people went to adore the calf as far as Dan.
And he made temples in the high places, and priests of the lowest of the people, who were not of the sons of Levi.

And he appointed a feast in the eighth month, on the fifteenth day of the month, after the manner of the feast that was celebrated in Juda. And going up to the altar, he did in like manner in Bethel, to sacrifice to the calves, which he had made: and he placed in Bethel priests of the high places, which he had made.

And he went up to the altar, which he had built in Bethel, on the fifteenth day of the eighth month, which he had devised of his own heart: and he ordained a feast to the children of Israel, and went up on the altar to burn incense.
And behold there came a man of God out of Juda, by the word of the Lord, to Bethel, when Jeroboam was standing upon the altar, and burning incense.

And he cried out against the altar in the word of the Lord, and said: O altar, altar, thus saith the Lord: Behold a child shall be born to the house of David, Josias by name, and he shall immolate upon thee the priests of the high places, who now burn incense upon thee, and he shall burn men's bones upon thee.
And he gave a sign the same day, saying: This shall be the sign, that the Lord hath spoken: Behold the altar shall be rent, and the ashes that are upon it, shall be poured out.

And when the king had heard the word of the man of God, which he had cried out against the altar in Bethel, he stretched forth his hand from the altar, saying: Lay hold on him. And his hand which he stretched forth against him, withered: and he was not able to draw it back again to him.
The altar also was rent, and the ashes were poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had given before in the word of the Lord.

And the king said to the man of God: Entreat the face of the Lord thy God, and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me. And the man of God besought the face of the Lord, and the king's hand was restored to him, and it became as it was before.
And the king said to the man of God: Come home with me to dine, and I will make thee presents.
And the man of God answered the king: If thou wouldst give me half thy house, I will not go with thee, nor eat bread, nor drink water in this place:
For so it was enjoined me by the word of the Lord commanding me: Thou shalt not eat bread, nor drink water, nor return by the same way that thou camest.
So he departed by another way, and returned not by the way that he came into Bethel.

Now a certain old prophet dwelt in Bethel, and his sons came to him, and told him all the works that the man of God had done that day in Bethel: and they told their father the words which he had spoken to the king.
And their father said to them: What way went he? His sons shewed him the way by which the man of God went, who came out of Juda.
And he said to his sons: Saddle me the ass. And when they had saddled it, he got up,
And went after the man of God, and found him sitting under a turpentine tree: and he said to him: Art thou the man of God who camest from Juda? He answered: I am.
And he said to him: Come home with me to eat bread.
But he said: I must not return, nor go with thee, neither will I eat bread, or drink water in this place:
Because the Lord spoke to me, in the word of the Lord, saying: Thou shalt not eat bread, and thou shalt not drink water there, nor return by the way thou wentest.

He said to him: I also am a prophet like unto thee: and an angel spoke to me, in the word of the Lord, saying: Bring him back with thee into thy house, that he may eat bread, and drink water. He deceived him, An angel spoke to me, etc... This old man of Bethel was indeed a prophet, but he sinned in thus deceiving the man of God; the more because he pretended a revelation for what he did.
And brought him back with him: so he ate bread, and drank water in his house.
And as they sat at table, the word of the Lord came to the prophet that brought him back:

And he cried out to the man of God who came out of Juda, saying: Thus saith the Lord: Because thou hast not been obedient to the Lord, and hast not kept the commandment which the Lord thy God commanded thee,

And hast returned, and eaten bread, and drunk water in the place wherein he commanded thee that thou shouldst not eat bread, nor drink water, thy dead body shall not be brought into the sepulchre of thy fathers.
And when he had eaten and drunk, he saddled his ass for the prophet, whom he had brought back.

And when he was gone, a lion found him in the way, and killed him, and his body was cast in the way: and the ass stood by him, and the lion stood by the dead body. Killed him... Thus the Lord often punishes his servants here, that he may spare them hereafter. For the generality of divines are of opinion, that the sin of this prophet, considered with all its circumstances, was not mortal.
And behold, men passing by, saw the dead body cast in the way, and the lion standing by the body. And they came and told it in the city, wherein that old prophet dwelt.

And when that prophet, who had brought him back out of the way, heard of it, he said: It is the man of God, that was disobedient to the mouth of the Lord, and the Lord hath delivered him to the lion, and he hath torn him, and killed him, according to the word of the Lord, which he spoke to him.
And he said to his sons: Saddle me an ass. And when they had saddled it,
And he was gone, he found the dead body cast in the way, and the ass and the lion standing by the carcass: the lion had not eaten of the dead body, nor hurt the ass.
And the prophet took up the body of the man of God, and laid it upon the ass, and going back brought it into the city of the old prophet, to mourn for him.
And he laid his dead body in his own sepulchre: and they mourned over him, saying: Alas! alas, my brother.
And when they had mourned over him, he said to his sons: When I am dead, bury me in the sepulchre wherein the man of God is buried: lay my bones beside his bones.

For assuredly the word shall come to pass which he hath foretold in the word of the Lord, against the altar that is in Bethel: and against all the temples of the high places, that are in the cities of Samaria.

After these words, Jeroboam came not back from his wicked way: but on the contrary, he made of the meanest of the people priests of the high places: whosoever would, he filled his hand, and he was made a priest of the high places.
And for this cause did the house of Jeroboam sin, and was cut off, and destroyed from the face of the earth.

lines: In those days again, when there was great multitude and they had nothing to eat; calling his disciples together, he saith to them:
I have compassion on the multitude, for behold they have now been with me three days and have nothing to eat.
And if I shall send them away fasting to their home, they will faint in the way: for some of them came from afar off.
And his disciples answered him: From whence can any one fill them here with bread in the wilderness?
And he asked them: How many loaves have ye? Who said: Seven.
And he commanded the people to sit down on the ground. And taking the seven loaves, giving thanks, he broke and gave to his disciples for to set before them. And they set them before the people.
And they had a few little fishes: and he blessed them and commanded them to be set before them.
And they did eat and were filled: and they took up that which was left of the fragments, seven baskets.
And they that had eaten were about four thousand. And he sent them away.
And immediately going up into a ship with his disciples, he came into the parts of Dalmanutha.
